ops.text: Vendor shall defend, indemnify, and hold harmless Customer and its Affiliates from and against any third-party claim, and all resulting damages, costs, and expenses (including reasonable attorneys' fees), to the extent arising out of (a) an allegation that the Services or Deliverables infringe or misappropriate any intellectual property right; (b) Vendor's breach of Applicable Law; (c) unauthorized access to or disclosure of Customer Data caused by Vendor; or (d) Vendor's gross negligence or wilful misconduct. Customer shall give Vendor written notice of the claim, Vendor shall control its defence and settlement, and Customer shall provide reasonable cooperation. Any indemnity given by Customer under this Agreement is limited to third-party claims arising from content Customer provides to Vendor and Customer's breach of Applicable Law.

quote: 9.3 Customer may terminate an Order Form immediately if Vendor suffers a material Security Incident, repeatedly misses a critical service level, violates Applicable Law in performing the Services, or infringes a third party's intellectual property and cannot provide the remedies required by Section 20.5.
rationale: The Agreement has no indemnity provision: Section 20 is absent entirely, and the only references to indemnity are cross-references (Section 9.3 points to a non-existent Section 20.5; Sections 19.4, 21.3 and 30.5 assume indemnification obligations exist). With no Vendor IP indemnity, the clause sits in walk-away territory. We inserted a preferred-level Vendor defence and indemnity (IP infringement by Services or Deliverables, Vendor's breach of Applicable Law, Vendor-caused Customer Data breach, gross negligence/wilful misconduct) with notice, control and cooperation, plus a limit on any Customer indemnity. We targeted preferred rather than fallback because Section 21.3 already treats indemnification obligations as Excluded Claims (uncapped); importing the fallback 3x super-cap would reduce our existing protection.

Retained Sections 9.3, 19.5 and 21.3 are untouched. quote: 14.2 Vendor exclusively owns every Deliverable created for Customer. Customer receives a revocable, non-transferable licence to use a Deliverable only during the applicable Order Form term.
rationale: Section 14.1 (Customer Data ownership, with Vendor's processing right confined to providing, securing, supporting and improving the Services for Customer), 14.3 (Vendor retains Vendor Technology; embedded Vendor Technology carried by the perpetual licence in 13.2) and 14.4 (no joint ownership) are all acceptable. Section 14.2, however, gives Vendor exclusive ownership of every Deliverable we pay to have created and leaves us only a revocable, non-transferable licence lasting no longer than the Order Form term. That fails even the fallback, which requires a perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free licence to use, modify and sublicense Deliverables — the 13.2 perpetual licence reaches only software and Vendor Technology, not the Deliverable itself. Because the remaining preferred elements are already satisfied elsewhere in Section 14 and 13.2, the shortest complete cure is to flip 14.2 to Customer ownership with an express assignment, reaching the preferred position in a single edit.

verification.notes: The preferred checklist is position-complete: the single edit to 14.2 supplies Customer ownership plus an express present-tense assignment of each Deliverable, and the remaining preferred elements are already satisfied by retained 13.2 (perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free embedded-IP licence), 14.1 (Customer Data ownership with processing limited to service delivery), 14.3 (Vendor retains Vendor Technology) and 14.4 (no joint ownership). The fallback level is not complete because the four Deliverable-licence attributes and the use/modify/sublicense rights are not expressed anywhere; that is immaterial since the preferred level is met and ownership is the stronger outcome, but the finding should not be characterised as resting on the fallback. Minimal: the edit replaces only the two offending sentences of 14.2 (Vendor exclusive ownership; revocable, non-transferable, term-limited licence) and adds nothing outside the checklist — no survival tail, no expense or procedure language, no duplication of the 13.2 licence. Preserves intent: 14.3's cross-reference to the Section 13.2 perpetual licence and 13.2's "embedded in a Deliverable" trigger both still operate; Vendor's identification and third-party-material restrictions, the feedback mechanics in 14.4 and the 1.4/1.8 definitions are untouched, leaving no dangling reference or contradictory retained sentence. Deterministic gates are consistent with substance: no assignment of Customer IP or Customer Data to Vendor survives, and the operation is the shortest route to a complete level. Classification of the original clause as a deviation is correct — original 14.2 gave Vendor exclusive ownership of paid-for Deliverables with only a revocable, non-transferable, term-limited licence back, failing even the fallback.

quote: 21.1 Except for Excluded Claims, each Party's total aggregate liability arising out of or relating to this Agreement shall not exceed the greater of the Fees paid or payable by Customer during the twelve months preceding the event giving rise to the claim and USD 1,000,000. The cap is mutual and applies regardless of the form of action or number of claims.
rationale: Section 21 meets our preferred position on all material terms. The cap in 21.1 is expressly mutual ("each Party's total aggregate liability"; "The cap is mutual") and is set at the greater of Fees paid or payable in the twelve months preceding the event giving rise to the claim and USD 1,000,000. "Fees" (1.5) covers recurring subscription, professional services and usage fees under Order Forms, so the basis is meaningful rather than illusory. 21.2 excludes indirect/consequential damages mutually ("neither Party is liable"), and helpfully confirms data-restoration, replacement-service, notice and incident-response costs are direct damages. 21.3 puts confidentiality, data-protection and security breaches, indemnification obligations, gross negligence, wilful misconduct, fraud, and infringement of the other Party's IP wholly outside the cap, with no indemnity sub-cap anywhere else in the document (19.4/19.5 preserve rather than limit those remedies). 21.4 is standard savings language and does not cut back the carve-outs. One point short of the ideal preferred wording, noted but not redlined: the payment carve-out in 21.3 reaches "undisputed Fees for conforming Services" rather than all Customer amounts due (Fees excludes taxes, expenses and interest). That is a minor sub-element and does not affect the fallback, every element of which is met.

quote: 24.1 Customer may assign this Agreement or an Order Form without Vendor's consent to an Affiliate or to a successor in a merger, reorganization, acquisition, or sale of all or substantially all assets or business to which the Agreement relates.
rationale: Section 24 meets our preferred position. 24.1 lets Customer assign to an Affiliate or to a successor in a merger, reorganization, acquisition or sale of substantially all assets without Vendor's consent (notice only). 24.2 bars Vendor from assigning, delegating material performance, or transferring by change of control without Customer's prior written consent, not unreasonably withheld, and bars assignment to a direct Customer competitor. 24.3 applies a mutual not-unreasonably-withheld consent standard to other assignments, and 24.4 expressly denies Vendor any termination, suspension, repricing, acceleration or service-reduction right on Customer's change of control; 13.3 confirms Customer's licence rights travel with a permitted assignment. The only wording short of preferred is that the competitor bar in 24.2 is qualified by "without Customer's consent" — a gate Customer itself controls — which we note but do not redline.

quote: Vendor acknowledges that Customer has made no exclusivity, non-compete, most-favoured-customer, minimum-volume, or no-hire commitment.
rationale: The Agreement imposes no exclusivity or sole-supplier obligation on Customer, so the rule sits at the preferred position. § 12.3 affirmatively preserves Customer's freedom to develop, acquire, license, sell or use any product or service and to engage any supplier, and records that Customer has made no exclusivity commitment. A document-wide search for exclusivity language ("exclusive", sole supplier, requirements, "shall not procure from any third party") returns only non-exclusive licence grants (§ 13.1), Vendor's ownership of Deliverables (§ 14.2), exclusive-remedy and exclusive-jurisdiction provisions — none of which restrict Customer's sourcing. § 7.2 (disclose-and-match before engaging another provider) is a right-to-match mechanic that does not prohibit Customer from using an alternative provider once honoured, so it belongs under MFN, not EXCLUSIVITY; § 2.1's take-or-pay volume floor is a minimum-commitment issue and is flagged under MINCOMMIT. No redline proposed under this rule.

quote: Vendor may not impose a platform, support, administration, minimum-use, or similar charge that the Order Form does not identify.
rationale: The Agreement imposes no liquidated damages, penalty, early-termination fee, minimum fee on termination, or Fee acceleration on Customer, so the preferred position (Customer pays no liquidated damages or penalties) is met. Section 7.1 bars unidentified minimum-use or similar charges; Section 27.3 lets Customer terminate "without penalty"; Section 24.4 bars acceleration of Fees on Customer change of control; and Section 10.2 provides refunds rather than exit charges. The only Customer-payable amounts on the money side are Fees for Services, reimbursable pre-approved expenses, and, under Section 22.2, reasonable audit costs plus the undisputed shortfall where an audit shows underpayment exceeding five percent — a cost-reimbursement and true-up mechanic, not a stipulated damages amount. The Section 2.1 take-or-pay commitment is economically similar in effect but is a minimum volume commitment reviewed under MINCOMMIT; we do not flag it twice here. No redline proposed.

quote: 13.3 Customer may transfer its licence rights to an Affiliate or successor in connection with an assignment permitted by Section 24. Vendor shall not revoke or suspend a licence except during a material uncured payment or use breach affecting the licensed item, after notice and a reasonable opportunity to cure.
rationale: The licence package meets the preferred position in full. § 13.1 grants the subscription right to "Customer, its Affiliates, and contractors acting on their behalf" (affiliates and contractors elements). § 13.2 grants a "perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free, fully paid licence" for paid-up software and Vendor Technology, including material embedded in a Deliverable (perpetual and irrevocable elements). § 13.3 limits Vendor revocation or suspension to a "material uncured payment or use breach affecting the licensed item, after notice and a reasonable opportunity to cure" (subscription licence terminable only for uncured material breach) and permits transfer to an Affiliate or successor in connection with an assignment permitted by § 24, which § 24.1 confirms includes merger, reorganization, acquisition, or sale of all or substantially all assets without Vendor consent (successor transferability). "Affiliate" is defined in § 1.1 as a controlled/controlling/commonly controlled entity, so affiliate coverage is genuine and needs no written-notice fallback mechanic. The revocable, non-transferable Deliverable licence in § 14.2 is inconsistent in tone, but § 13.3's no-revocation rule and § 14.3's carry-through of the § 13.2 perpetual licence to Vendor Technology needed to use a Deliverable preserve our position; that Deliverable ownership/licence point is a Section 14 IP issue and we do not flag it twice here.

rationale: Section 19 clears the fallback and in substance nearly all of the preferred checklist. 19.1 warrants Services are performed in a professional and workmanlike manner and that Services and Deliverables materially conform to documentation and specifications; 19.2 gives a ninety-day Deliverable conformance warranty running from the later of delivery or acceptance and warrants Hosted Services will conform throughout the subscription term (well beyond the 30-day services floor and, for the hosted software, longer than the preferred 12 months); 19.3 adds malicious-code and Applicable Law compliance warranties; and 19.4 supplies the full remedy ladder of re-performance/repair/replacement followed by termination and refund of Fees paid, expressly non-exclusive for fraud, infringement, confidentiality, privacy, security and indemnified claims. 19.5 confirms no disclaimer limits an express warranty, so the disclaimer does not swallow the warranty. The only preferred sub-element short of the mark is that non-hosted Deliverables carry 90 days rather than 12 months; that is a minor gap noted here rather than redlined, since the clause otherwise sits at or above the fallback with the same remedies.
